steps.ask: How do people come into the study?

options.text: Everyone who walks a lane is counted, unless they ring the bell to say no.
options.note: Almost everyone is counted. Most of them never heard the bell explained, and do not know they are in a study.

options.text: A keeper at each bell explains the study, and people sign a slip if they agree.
options.note: About half agree. Night workers and the hill families are mostly missing: they pass the bells when no keeper is there.

options.text: Forty households are chosen by lot, visited, and asked.
options.note: Only forty households, but the lot reaches every district, including the hill families and the night shift.

options.text: Only counts: how many people pass each lane in each hour.
options.note: The council learns where the lanes are busy. Nobody can be followed from lane to lane.

options.text: Each person's route, under a token number instead of a name.
options.note: The council learns how people move across the city. On a quiet lane at night, a token number can point to one person.

options.text: Names and routes, so the council can ask people why they chose a lane.
options.note: The council can ask good follow-up questions. It can also see exactly where each named person goes.

options.text: The people who took part, at an open evening, before anyone else.
options.note: The people in the study can correct it before it is used. It takes a month longer.

options.text: The council, which decides what to do with the lanes.
options.note: The council can act quickly. The people in the study learn about it when the lanes change.

options.text: Everyone, on the public board in Library Dispatch.
options.note: Anyone can check the council's reading. Anyone can also read whatever the study kept.

warnings.line: Clerk Lin goes pale. 'Names and routes on the public board. Anyone could find out where anyone walks at night.'
Keeper Ade frowns. 'Token routes on a public board. On the quiet lanes, people will work out whose token is whose.'
Clerk Lin: 'So we would hold the names and routes of people who never knew they were in a study.'
